items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. That is a pretty good start for a tiny Meshtastic board. Affiliate disclosure: I may earn from qualifying purchases through the product link below. items.title: [redmondpie.com] Apple tells stores to inspect cracked iPhone Duo screens
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Apple has told its retail stores and authorized service providers to inspect iPhone Duo foldable phones with cracked inner displays and repair or replace them under standard procedures after acknowledging a problem affecting a “small number” of units. The phone went on sale Oct. 23, and owners began reporting cracks along the hinge within days, sometimes accompanied by bright lines across the screen. Apple says most units are unaffected but has not disclosed how many phones are affected or confirmed a cause. It has announced neither a recall nor a public repair program. A teardown by repair specialist iFixit suggested a hinge problem, but Apple has not confirmed that explanation. Owners experiencing the defect should contact AppleCare for a replacement. New online orders were estimated to arrive in January 2027.

items.title: [Fast Company] Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”

items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

PHP’s maintainers released fixes on Oct. 21 for two critical vulnerabilities that could let attackers run code on exposed web servers without logging in, prompting governments and companies to take websites offline while they applied patches. The flaws, rated 9.2 out of 10, affect PHP installations serving web requests; the PHP team released patched versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. Precautionary shutdowns affected public services and businesses in Europe, Australia and Asia. France disabled local-government sites, the Netherlands took its DigiD digital identity portal and parliamentary sites offline, and Japanese companies suspended some online services; Wikipedia’s operator also temporarily took supporting systems offline. PHP underpins an estimated 70% of websites, though only sites running PHP on their own servers are exposed. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws using AI tools in August, and details leaked online on Oct. 20, a day before the planned patch release. Cloudflare reported millions of exploitation attempts after disclosure, while Amazon said it detected an attempt against a decoy system on Oct. 17; reports described attempts but no confirmed successful exploitation at that point. Agencies advised organizations to patch promptly or isolate vulnerable systems until they could apply the fixes.

items.title: [Fast Company] Town CEO Jean-Denis Greze on why most people still don’t know what to ask AI
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

AI agents are powerful, but most ordinary people don’t yet use them. Town wants to change that. Led by CEO Jean-Denis Greze, playfully referred to as Town’s mayor, the company announced a $108 million Series B on October 19, co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures, at a $1 billion valuation.  

Greze cofounded the San Francisco startup with Tony Vincent in late 2024 after serving as CTO of Plaid, where he built up the engineering team from about 20 people to 350.

Town’s betting it can make AI more accessible and practical for small-business owners and mid-market firms still looking for day-to-day AI benefits. 

Fast Company spoke with Greze about why most people still treat AI like a fancy search engine, where AI assistants can be most helpful, and why he’s working harder than he ever has before. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

ChatGPT and Claude can already connect to other apps. Why do people need stand-alone AI assistants like yours?

Could Claude or ChatGPT do most of what Town does? I think the answer is, most of it, yeah, they can. But most people who use ChatGPT or Claude aren’t using those tools to do what people in tech describe as agentic work, which just means using them to actually do things for you as opposed to researching things for you. They use it more as a Google Search replacement.

I think the biggest reason is that most people don’t really know what to put in the chat box. Putting someone in front of an empty box and asking them to write what to do, especially when the capabilities are changing all the time—that’s not onboarding.

No one’s figured out how you take a mainstream person and get them to use these products to their full potential. That’s the market opportunity. And we may be wrong, by the way. Maybe distribution just wins, and Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI end up winning. As a startup, that’s the risk you’re taking on.

What’s a use case that surprised you?

There’s a small travel firm at a vacation destination where people rent cars and gear, like a bike, for the day. The business is totally run over email. If something’s damaged, the employee takes pictures and sends an email to the central processing person.

Now there’s a little workflow that at the end of the day takes all the emails with the pictures, looks at the CRM for who the people are, and drafts the emails. They were drafting 10 to 12 of these emails every day, and it wasted 25 minutes; now it takes them 5 minutes. No one’s building SaaS for that small business. 

What should we call this category of tool? An AI assistant? A chief of staff?

We call our product a Townie. If you use the word assistant or the phrase chief of staff, you have a human mental model for what an assistant does. I think what this technology does today and what it’ll do in five years will probably defy these expectations. And no one knows what a chief of staff does outside of CEOs of Fortune 500 companies.

I actually think the right analogy for what we’re building is more like a browser or a device. When the App Store came out, suddenly a percentage of what you used to do in your web browser, you started to just do in your phone. Adding AI assistance is the same. 

The percentage of the time you interact with information in a browser or your phone will just go down now forever, and the percentage that you do by talking to an AI will go up. The future, I think, is voice for sure.

What’s next for Town?

I’m very excited about live voice. You could imagine in the morning you’re commuting to work and you have in your ear a world-class executive assistant that’s telling you, “Hey, you got seven emails overnight. There’s two of them that are urgent. On this one, if you tell me this, I can help draft the reply. The other one is going to require you to move a meeting later today. Do you want me to come up with some options?” It’s just talking to you, and you can interrupt it.

I’m also excited about what we call agent to agent. You could say, “Who at the company is really close with someone doing R&D at this other company?” Your agent will talk to other agents at your own company, and it’ll learn that Bob plays tennis with someone there. But it won’t tell you that. It’ll just be like, “Hey, Bob appears to be closely connected to that person. Do you want me to ask them if they can do the intro?” Leveraging the network of everyone within a company in a way that’s privacy-preserving is huge.

Should people connect their financial accounts to an AI agent?

If you’re a consumer, it is very likely that you connect everything about you, your medicals, your financials, to the agents. It’s just too beneficial. It’ll tell you that your credit card rate’s too high, that you should apply for a different one. It’s free money.

But the privacy concern is real. I don’t think you want to use an assistant where you’re not convinced it’s making decisions that are in your best interest. These products only work in a world where you think they truly have your best interest.

Can you trust those services?

If you’re paying for it, you can. If you’re not paying for a service, you’re not the customer. You’re being monetized in some other way.

We made the choice very early: We like consumer use cases, and they’re subsidized by business use cases. We charge businesses, and it’s not a cheap product; it’s not $5 a month. Our main plan is $50 a month.

What’s the hardest part of running Town?

The world’s too fast. I’ve never seen anything like it. It’s nerve-racking. Software had high gross margins because there was a really high fixed cost to copying it, and there was a real advantage to being early in market. By the time someone could copy you, you’d have built the next feature.

With AI, competition moves so fast and good ideas are copied so quickly. Things that would take nine months to copy are copied in a month or two.

So the pressure you feel to execute and to work a lot—I’m 47, but I’ve not worked this hard [before]. Psychologically, it’s tough, because you’re either ecstatic because you shipped something before OpenAI did, or you’re in fear that there’s a tweet from Sam Altman that puts you on your back foot. So that’s super stressful.

How do you use Town outside of work?

I’ve told Town to research food blogs and newspapers that write about food in San Francisco. I have a date night with my wife every Sunday night. Perspective: Ryan Ness, adaptation research director at the Canadian Climate Institute: Ness said federal climate action is not keeping pace with climate change and recent policy shifts have made Canada’s net-zero commitment harder to reach (insideclimatenews.org). (Inside Climate News)
Quote: "Canada’s evidence will show that global climate change requires a global solution" (BJ Wray, counsel for Canada’s Department of Justice, Winnipeg Free Press)
Timeline: 2020: A federal trial court dismissed the case before evidence was heard (grist.org).
Timeline: 2023: The Federal Court of Appeal allowed revised Section 7 claims to proceed (grist.org).
Timeline: 26 October 2026: The youth-led climate trial opened at the federal courthouse in Vancouver (winnipegfreepress.com, thestar.com).
Timeline: February 2027: Closing arguments are scheduled after the evidentiary hearings (grist.org, sudouest.fr).

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.

The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.

Bibi Rajinder Kaur, a Sikh, donated family land to build a mosque in her village. ‘There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,’ she says

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Missing blood pressure medication could mean losing much of its protection against heart attacks and strokes, according to an analysis of more than 91,000 people. Patients who consistently took their medication experienced an 11% reduction in major cardiovascular events, while those who missed too many doses saw little or no measurable benefit.
